source_tasks.problem: The expression $4 \times  5 +  2 -  8 -  3 +  3 \times  5$ may be changed only by inserting parentheses; rearranging numbers or operations is not allowed. In total, how many values can be obtained?

Consider the expression $4 +  8 -  6 \cdot  6 -  4 +  2 \cdot  7$. Fully parenthesize it in every possible way without changing the order of numbers or operations. Parenthesizations with the same numerical result count only once. How many distinct values are possible?
The expression $7 +  6 \times  8 -  6 +  5 \times  3 -  5$ may be changed only by inserting parentheses; rearranging numbers or operations is not allowed. In total, how many values can be obtained?

interface_note: Only parameter values vary; all mathematical conditions and requested quantity remain those stated by the supplied source questions. Names describe source data, not a target algorithm. Implement solve(parameters), no natural-language applicability detection. operators must have exactly len(operands)-1 entries.

analysis.invalid_operation: Manually enumerating a subset of parenthesizations and/or hand-maintaining a union list of values, then reporting its size (or guessing a plausible number such as 116) without exhaustively computing the interval-DP sets.
observations: All three source tasks ask for the number of distinct values obtainable by fully parenthesizing a fixed sequence of operands and binary operators (+,-,*), preserving order.
The attempted solutions either enumerate parenthesizations by hand (error-prone, truncated) or use interval DP but then miscount or misreport the union of value sets.

The failing pattern is not the DP recurrence itself but the final aggregation: manual enumeration misses cases, and hand-maintained union lists are unreliable; one attempt even guessed a 'nice' number (116) without computation.
The correct mathematical object is well-defined: for each interval [i,j], the set of achievable values is the union over splits k of {a op_k b : a in S(i,k), b in S(k+1,j)}; the answer is |S(0,n-1)|.
The interface guarantees operators has exactly len(operands)-1 entries, so the DP is directly implementable with exact integer arithmetic.
analysis.procedure_plan: Implement solve(operands, operators): let n=len(operands). Build a 2D table S[i][j] of sets of integers. Base case S[i][i]={operands[i]}. For length L=2..n, for each i with j=i+L-1, initialize empty set; for each split k from i to j-1, for each a in S[i][k] and b in S[k+1][j], apply operators[k] (+,-,*) to get v and add to the set. Use Python sets of ints (exact arithmetic, no floats). Return len(S[0][n-1]). This deterministically enumerates all full parenthesizations via the standard interval DP and deduplicates by set union, so the count is exact. Complexity is bounded by the number of distinct subexpression values, which is small for n<=8.
analysis.replacement_operation: Compute the exact set of achievable values via interval DP: S[i][j] = union over k of {a op_k b : a in S[i][k], b in S[k+1][j]}, with S[i][i]={operands[i]}, and return the cardinality of S[0][n-1]. This replaces sampling/guessing with exhaustive set-based enumeration, which is the logically correct way to count distinct results.
analysis.uncertainty: The DP recurrence is standard and trustworthy; the main residual risk is performance if intermediate value sets grow large, but with n<=8 and small integer operands this is negligible. There is no ambiguity in the requested quantity: full parenthesizations preserving order, counting distinct numerical results once. The prior failures are attributable to manual enumeration/guessing and to hand-aggregation errors, not to a flaw in the DP formulation, so confidence in the proposed procedure is high.
